current_episode.title: How to Become a Leader in Digital Engineering with Devon Middleditch

guest.titre: Head of Digital Engineering and Technology
guest.bio_context: Devon Middleditch has worked as a leader at Tier 1 companies including AECOM and held roles in government agencies such as Transport for New South Wales. He relocated from New Zealand to Australia early in his career and was instrumental in developing digital engineering frameworks on major infrastructure programs. He has scaled teams, shaped organizational culture, and pioneered the adoption of emerging technologies including drones, augmented reality, and common data environments in linear infrastructure projects.

pending_qa.q: What early-career development helped Devon Middleditch succeed in transitioning from technical to leadership roles?
pending_qa.r: Two half-day training modules were transformative: Understanding Self and Others, and Managing Self and Others. These modules were like an epiphany because they taught that not everybody responds the same way in meetings—some people need to be prepared beforehand, some need to talk about it after, and some want to talk during. Understanding these concepts and different personas is invaluable when transitioning from technical to leadership roles.

pending_qa.q: What is the key difference between leadership in government agencies versus private engineering consulting firms?
pending_qa.r: Government agencies operate with more compliance-driven processes and political movements influencing agendas, whereas engineering consulting firms make decisions much quicker for deliberate business reasons. However, government agencies have greater scale and resources to invest in emerging technologies like autonomous vehicles, sustainability programs, robotics, and drones—things that engineering consultancies typically only explore on mega projects.

pending_qa.q: How should leaders define and maintain culture across teams experiencing rapid growth?
pending_qa.r: Culture means people feel valued, have a voice, enjoy coming to work, operate in an inclusive environment, and have autonomy. Leaders should be consistent in their approach so people know what to expect. Instead of relying on annual tick-box surveys, leaders should be in the weeds with people through water cooler chats, coffee conversations, and team events. How people operate under project pressure is a real testament to what the culture is like.

pending_qa.q: How does Devon Middleditch approach leading innovation teams versus project delivery teams differently?
pending_qa.r: People inventing the future operate differently from those delivering projects and design. Innovation teams do not like controls or constraints; they need big-picture thinking and space to operate. Trying to impose strict boundaries, program controls, or worrying about timesheets demotivates them. A leader must give them space and support while talking their language, whereas project delivery teams require different management approaches.

pending_qa.q: What workforce composition strategy maintains culture while scaling rapidly during high workload periods?
pending_qa.r: Devon recommends a 70-30 ratio of full-time employees to contingent workforce. When you have a strong core of FTE staff, the culture is maintained. When the balance reverses and you have 30% full-time employees and 70% contingent workforce, the culture erodes. The contingent workforce needs to be treated as part of the team to preserve organizational culture.

pending_qa.q: What was the career-defining moment that led to Devon Middleditch's leadership in digital engineering?
pending_qa.r: Devon wrote a paper to executives outlining Engineering 2.0 and the need to scale computing technology in engineering delivery. Initially receiving no feedback, he thought it was a career-limiting move. However, a Vice President of Operations parachuted into the Doha Expressway Program—the world's largest roads program building Qatar's World Cup road network—called him to discuss the paper and asked him to become the technology architect for the program.

pending_qa.q: What innovative technologies did Devon Middleditch implement on the Doha Expressway Program around 2010?
pending_qa.r: On the Doha Expressway Program, Devon implemented drones to verify if digging was occurring on the ground for progress payments, iPads with early augmented reality software to visualize where roads would be built in the sand dunes, a common data environment where every consultant fed into one database with security-based delineation of access, and a move from string-based CAD solutions to templated-type modeling tools.

pending_qa.q: What advice does Devon Middleditch give to early-career technical professionals aspiring to leadership?
pending_qa.r: If you are a technical person, it is easy to drift back to your safe space. Devon suggests taking professional development modules on understanding self and others, and managing self and others. It is also important to recognize that not everybody responds the same way and to understand different personas. This prevents you from leaning back into technical work and helps you embrace a genuine leadership scope.
